Here is a plain-prose analysis of the risk assessment.

When a legacy module like `config/legacy_flags.py` has no obvious current owner and appears unused, "unused" almost always means "not imported by anything currently under active development" rather than "genuinely dead." The gap between those two claims is where incidents happen. A static import scan across the primary codebase will confirm nothing references the module through normal Python imports, but it cannot see several categories of dependency that are common in exactly this kind of file.

First, dynamic access: code that reaches the module via `importlib`, `getattr`, string-based dotted paths in config files, plugin registries, or `__import__` calls built from a variable. Feature-flag modules are especially prone to this pattern because flags are often looked up by name from a central registry rather than imported directly by each call site.

Second, non-Python consumers: shell scripts, CI/CD pipelines, cron jobs, deployment manifests, or Terraform/Ansible playbooks that source values out of this file, parse it as data, or invoke it as a script. A grep across the whole repo (not just source directories) and across any infra-as-code repos is necessary, not optional.

Third, side effects at import time. Legacy flag modules sometimes register handlers, monkey-patch other modules, populate a global registry, or set environment defaults purely by being imported somewhere in the dependency graph — meaning even a single stray import elsewhere (test fixtures, a `conftest.py`, an `__init__.py`) can create a load-bearing effect invisible to a simple "who calls functions in this file" search.

Fourth, external and cross-repo consumers: internal libraries published to a package index, other services in a monorepo-adjacent repo, or downstream teams who vendored or copied logic referencing these flags. Grep is blind to anything outside the repo being searched.

Fifth, runtime/production-only paths: flags gated behind rare conditions (specific customer tiers, disaster-recovery mode, an admin override) that never fire in normal traffic or in the test suite, so removal looks safe in CI and staging but breaks an infrequent but real production path.

To assess risk before deleting, I would: run a full-text (not just import) search repo-wide and in adjacent repos; check production logs, metrics, or feature-flag dashboards for recent evaluation of any flags defined there; add temporary instrumentation (a deprecation warning or usage counter) and leave it running through at least one full business cycle, including month-end/quarter-end jobs that run infrequently; check version-control blame and any linked tickets for why it was introduced; and finally deprecate rather than delete outright — rename, log on access, or fail loudly in a non-critical way — for one release cycle before hard removal, so any silent dependency surfaces as a visible error instead of a silent failure.

Legacy modules like `config/legacy_flags.py` are dangerous to delete precisely because "unused" is hard to verify by inspection. Several categories of dependency can hide from a straightforward grep or IDE reference search.

First, dynamic access defeats static analysis. Python code frequently reads flags via `getattr`, `importlib`, string-keyed dict lookups, or `__import__` with a computed module name. A config module built around feature flags is especially likely to be touched this way — e.g., `getattr(legacy_flags, flag_name, default)` — which no "find usages" tool will catch.

Second, external and cross-process consumers. Cron jobs, deployment scripts, CI pipelines, admin tools, or a separate service (even in another repo) might import this module directly or shell out to a script that does. Config modules are also sometimes read by tooling outside the main application entirely — a Django `settings.py`, a Celery worker, a one-off data migration script, or an internal dashboard.

Third, indirect coupling through side effects. If the module executes code at import time (registers a flag with some global registry, monkey-patches a setting, sets an environment variable, populates a cache), other code may depend on that side effect having occurred rather than on any name defined in the module. Deleting it silently breaks the assumption even though nothing imports symbols from it directly.

Fourth, serialized or persisted references — flag names stored in a database, a feature-flag service, log parsing rules, or test fixtures that reference constants defined here. These won't show up in code search at all.

To assess risk before removal, I'd take a layered approach. Start with static analysis across the entire monorepo (not just the immediate service) for both direct imports and string-based references to the module name and its symbol names. Then check runtime signals: instrument the module to log on any access (attribute read, function call) and leave it running in production for a full business cycle — weekly/monthly batch jobs matter here — since "unused" claims are often based on someone's memory of the hot path, not actual telemetry. Search deploy scripts, cron tables, and CI/CD configs separately, since those often live outside the main codebase's search scope. Check version control history and blame to see who last touched it and why, which sometimes surfaces the original intent even if current owners don't understand it.

If instrumentation shows zero hits after a full cycle and no external references turn up, deletion is low-risk — but I'd still land it as a discrete, easily revertible commit, keep the file recoverable in history, and monitor error rates and any flag-dependent behavior for a few days after deploy rather than treating a clean search as final proof.

Legacy configuration modules like this are dangerous precisely because "unused" is hard to prove and easy to disprove after the fact. Config code differs from ordinary logic in that its call sites are often indirect: values get read via string-keyed lookups, environment variable fallbacks, dynamic imports, or reflection-style getattr calls that a static grep or IDE "find references" won't catch. A flag defined in legacy_flags.py might be imported once under an alias three layers removed from anywhere the word "legacy_flags" appears, or read by name from a settings dictionary assembled at runtime.

Several categories of hidden dependency are worth checking specifically. First, deployment and infrastructure: CI/CD pipelines, Docker entrypoints, or Kubernetes configmaps may set environment variables or mount files that only this module parses. Second, feature flags controlling rarely-exercised code paths — a flag gating a quarterly batch job, a disaster-recovery mode, or an admin-only feature won't show activity in normal test runs or production traffic sampling, but removing it could break that path silently until the day it's needed. Third, external or cross-team consumers: another service, a scheduled job, or a data pipeline maintained by a different team might import this module even though nobody on the current team wrote or reviewed that dependency. Fourth, backward-compatibility shims — code that translates an old config format to a new one for systems that haven't migrated.

To assess risk before deletion, I'd combine several evidence sources rather than trust any single one. Static analysis (grep/AST search across the entire monorepo, not just the current service) for both the module name and any flag names it defines, including as strings. Runtime evidence: code coverage or logging instrumentation added for a full deploy cycle (ideally spanning a release, a batch/cron cycle, and a peak-load period) to see if any line actually executes. Git blame and commit history to find the last meaningful change and whether it correlates with an incident. Search of build artifacts, generated documentation, and any service registry for consumers outside the current repo. And a deprecation warning added first — log a warning wherever the module is touched, ship it for a full cycle, and see if anything fires.

Given all that, I'd recommend a staged removal rather than a single deletion commit: first add loud runtime warnings when it's exercised, then after a clean observation window (long enough to span monthly/quarterly jobs), replace the module body with an error stub for one release rather than deleting the file outright, so any remaining dependency fails fast and visibly instead of silently. Only delete the file once that stub has gone through a full deploy cycle without triggering.

Legacy configuration modules like `config/legacy_flags.py` are risky to delete precisely because their dependencies are rarely expressed as visible imports alone. A 400-line flags file typically accumulates several categories of silent coupling. First, dynamic access: code elsewhere may reference flag names via `getattr`, string-keyed dictionary lookups, `globals()`, or reflection-based config loaders, none of which show up in a static import graph or a simple "who imports this" search. Second, side effects at import time: the module may register flags with a central registry, set environment variables, monkey-patch other modules, or run initialization code the moment it's imported, meaning downstream behavior depends on it having been loaded at all, independent of any specific symbol being used. Third, external and cross-boundary references: deployment scripts, CI pipelines, Terraform/Ansible configs, feature-flag dashboards, or other services might read values that originate from or mirror this module, especially if flag names are duplicated as environment variables or config keys elsewhere. Fourth, tests: a passing test suite doesn't prove non-use if the tests themselves mock out or stub the flags, or if coverage of the code paths gated by these flags is thin or absent. Fifth, conditional/dead-looking branches: flags controlling rare code paths (holiday sales logic, an emergency killswitch, a legacy data-migration fallback) may look unused simply because the triggering condition hasn't occurred recently, not because the path is truly dead.

A sound risk assessment would proceed in layers rather than trusting any single signal. Start with static analysis (grep across the full monorepo, not just the current package, including config files, YAML, and shell scripts, since flag names are often referenced as strings rather than imported symbols). Follow with dynamic verification: add deprecation warnings or logging inside the module and run it in production or staging for a full business cycle (including any cyclical/seasonal code paths) to catch runtime access that static analysis misses. Check version control history and commit messages for context on why the flags exist and whether they map to known incidents. Search issue trackers and internal docs for the module name. If available, use runtime coverage or telemetry tools to confirm which branches gated by these flags actually execute. Finally, treat deletion as reversible risk management rather than a one-shot decision: rename or quarantine the module first (e.g., move it behind a clearly marked deprecation shim that logs on access), keep it in a removable state for one or two release cycles, and only delete outright once the logging confirms zero touches across that window. This staged approach converts "nobody understands it" from a reason for anxiety into a solvable discovery problem, without requiring anyone to reconstruct tribal knowledge from memory before acting.

Removing an undocumented 400-line configuration module carries risk that is largely invisible to static analysis, because configuration code tends to be consumed indirectly rather than through explicit imports. The first category of risk is runtime string-based lookup: other parts of the system may reference flag names as strings — pulled from environment variables, database rows, feature-flag services, or dynamically constructed attribute lookups — meaning a simple "who imports this file" search will miss every caller. Second, serialized state can depend on it: if any of these flags were ever written into saved configs, database records, migration files, or cached objects, deserialization code may expect keys or defaults that only this module defines. Third, external interfaces may key off it silently — CLI argument parsers, admin panels, or API request handlers might branch on flag values without the module's name appearing anywhere near the branch. Fourth, test suites and CI scripts often import fixtures or constants from legacy modules specifically because nobody wanted to duplicate them, so deletion can break builds without breaking production. Fifth, and most insidious, disabled or "off" code paths may still reference these flags for their default values; removing the module could silently flip behavior rather than throwing an error, which is far more dangerous than a crash.

To assess the actual risk, start with static tooling: full-repository search (not just imports) for the module's filename, its individual flag names, and common access patterns like getattr or dictionary lookups against a settings dict it might populate. Follow with dynamic evidence: add logging or a deprecation warning inside the module in a non-production environment and observe whether it fires under a realistic workload, then extend that instrumentation to a canary or staging deployment over a period long enough to catch weekly and monthly batch jobs, not just daily traffic. Check version control history for the original context — commit messages and old pull requests often explain why a flag exists even after the reasoning has left institutional memory. Search infrastructure-as-code, environment files, and any external config store for references to the same flag names, since the dependency may live entirely outside the codebase. Finally, treat the removal as reversible rather than final: delete behind a feature flag or in a branch that sits in production alongside the original for one full deploy cycle, with alerting on any code path that still touches it, before deleting outright. If after all of that nothing fires, the risk is low, but "nobody understands it" is itself information — it means whoever could explain the edge cases is no longer available to answer questions when something breaks quietly weeks later.

Removing an undocumented 400-line configuration module is less risky in terms of what breaks immediately and more risky in terms of what breaks invisibly, weeks or months later, in a form nobody connects back to the deletion. The core danger with legacy flag modules is that their consumers are often indirect: other code doesn't call the module, it calls a wrapper, reads an environment-derived default, or imports a constant that happens to originate there. Static analysis (grep, import graphs, IDE "find usages") catches direct references but misses dynamic access — dictionary lookups by string key, `getattr` calls, config loaded through a plugin registry, or values re-exported under a different name in some `__init__.py`. It also misses anything reached only by a rarely-run code path: a holiday billing cycle, a disaster-recovery script, a monthly batch job, an admin-only feature flag toggle. A module can appear completely unused for the entire time anyone's watching and still be the only thing controlling behavior in a situation that hasn't occurred yet during the observation window.

There's also a distinction between "nothing imports this" and "nothing depends on this." Even if imports are clean, the module might set process-wide state as a side effect of being imported at all — registering a handler, mutating a global dict, setting an environment variable other code reads later. Deleting it silently changes that state rather than raising an error, which is worse than a crash because it fails quietly.

To assess this properly, I'd want several independent signals before trusting any one of them. First, exhaustive static reference search, including string-based and reflective lookups, not just import statements. Second, runtime evidence: instrument the module (log statements, or a lightweight tripwire that records every attribute access) and leave it running across a full business cycle — ideally a full year if seasonal logic is plausible — before concluding it's dormant. Third, version-control archaeology: read the commit history and any associated tickets to understand why it was introduced, since "nobody understands it" often means "the person who wrote it left" rather than "it does nothing." Fourth, check deployment and packaging configuration, not just source code — sometimes a file is referenced by a build script, a Docker layer, or a config-loading mechanism external to the Python import system.

Given all that, I'd treat deletion as a staged process rather than a single commit: first deprecate with loud warnings, then disable behind a flag with a fast rollback path, monitor a full cycle, and only then delete. That sequencing converts an irreversible guess into a reversible experiment, which matters most exactly when institutional knowledge about the code is gone.

Cleanup commits fail differently from feature commits: there's no new behavior to test, so the review instinct that normally catches bugs — "does this do what it's supposed to?" — has nothing to grab onto. The actual risk in a cleanup diff isn't in what was added, it's in the assumption that everything removed was truly unreachable. That assumption breaks in a handful of predictable ways.

Dead code often isn't dead, it's dormant. A code path with no visible caller in the current codebase can still be invoked by a feature flag, an A/B test bucket, a scheduled job, a webhook handler, or a rare error-recovery branch that only fires under load or on retry. Static analysis and IDE "find usages" miss anything invoked through reflection, dependency injection, string-based routing, or dynamic imports. CSS is worse: a class that appears unused because no template references it directly may still be applied by JavaScript at runtime, by a third-party script, by an email template, or by a print stylesheet — and browsers fail silently when a rule is missing, so there's no error to surface the problem until a user hits a now-unstyled or now-nonfunctional element.

The checkout flow specifically is a common victim because it's disproportionately dependent on code paths that are rare in day-to-day testing: specific payment methods, specific currencies, guest checkout versus logged-in checkout, mobile web versus desktop, cart states with promo codes or gift cards. A cleanup pass that looks safe against the paths an engineer exercises manually can be silently removing something that only the 2% edge case touches — and checkout edge cases are exactly where revenue concentrates disproportionately, so the blast radius is bigger than the code size suggests.

The review practices that catch this share a common thread: they replace "does this look unused" with "can we prove it's unused." Concretely:

- Runtime usage data, not just static grep. Instrumenting suspected-dead code with logging or metrics for a full business cycle (covering weekly/monthly batch jobs, not just a few days) before deleting it turns "looks unused" into "confirmed unused."
- Feature-flag and config audits as a separate step from code search, since flag-gated code won't show up as "referenced" in the way reviewers expect.
- Treating checkout, payments, and auth as protected zones requiring elevated review and a full regression pass regardless of how trivial the diff looks — the risk classification should be based on the code's blast radius, not the size or apparent triviality of the change.
- Staged rollout (canary or percentage-based) for any change touching critical paths, even pure deletions, so a break shows up as a monitoring alert on a small slice of traffic instead of a full outage.
- A rollback plan defined before merge, not improvised during the incident.

The underlying discipline is to size review effort to consequence, not to diff size. A three-line CSS deletion in checkout deserves more scrutiny than a five-hundred-line refactor in an internal admin tool.

Cleanup commits fail differently than feature commits, which is what makes them dangerous: reviewers approach them with lowered guard, since "removing things" feels inherently safer than "adding things." That asymmetry in scrutiny is the root cause more often than any technical factor.

Three mechanisms recur in incidents like this. First, dead code often isn't dead — it's reachable through a path the static analysis or grep-based audit didn't see: a feature flag, a rare error branch, a reflection-based call, a cron job that runs monthly, or a dependency injected at runtime rather than referenced directly. Code that looks unused from a text search can be load-bearing for a fraction of traffic that simply hasn't hit it during the observation window used to justify the cleanup. Second, "unused" CSS is frequently a false negative from tooling. Coverage-based unused-CSS detection only sees the states it actually exercised; it misses hover, focus, error, print, and JS-toggled classes. A selector removed because it "matched nothing" during a crawl may be the exact rule that keeps a checkout button clickable or a modal from covering the page in one particular browser or viewport. Third, cleanup PRs are typically large in diff count but low in perceived risk, so they get a fast rubber-stamp review — nobody re-derives why each line existed, they just check that nothing obviously broke in a quick look.

The checkout-specific failure mode is usually one of these landing together: a CSS class thought unused was actually gating visibility or layout on a step of the flow, or a helper function or import removed as dead code was in fact the fallback path used when a payment provider's primary integration errors — a path that only fires under specific conditions rare enough to be invisible in a week of traffic logs.

Practices that catch this before production:

Treat deletions as changes requiring the same evidence bar as additions — "why is this safe to remove" needs its own justification, not just "it wasn't in the coverage report." Grep for string references, dynamic imports, and configuration lookups, not just static call graphs. Cross-check unused-CSS tooling against multiple crawl sessions covering interactive states, not a single pass. Run the change through a full staging pass of the affected flow, not just a smoke test, because checkout in particular tends to have provider-specific and state-dependent branches. Stage the rollout — feature-flag or canary deletions on high-value flows so a bad removal affects a small percentage of traffic before affecting all of it. Finally, keep a fast, well-drilled rollback path, since the honest goal isn't preventing every bad cleanup but shrinking the time between "it broke" and "it's reverted."

Cleanup commits fail because "dead" and "unused" are runtime claims disguised as static observations, and the codebase rarely gives you enough evidence to verify them. A function looks unreachable because nothing in the visible call graph invokes it — but reflection, dependency injection, cron jobs, feature flags, or a separate service calling through a public API can all reach code that a text search or even a decent static analyzer won't find. CSS is worse: a class selector with zero matches in the current templates can still be the target of JavaScript that adds it conditionally, an email-generation module rendered elsewhere, or a class computed dynamically from a string template that no grep will catch. The removal is safe in every code path the author checked and unsafe in the one they didn't.

Checkout flows are especially exposed to this because they tend to be old, high-traffic, and composed of code from several eras: a legacy discount calculator nobody touches, a CSS class that only activates during a specific promo or payment-method combination, a "deprecated" endpoint still hit by a mobile app version still in the wild. The very fact that this code is rarely modified — which made it look safe to remove — is often exactly why nobody remembered it was live.

There's also a scope problem specific to cleanup PRs: because the diff reads as subtractive and low-risk, it gets less scrutiny than a feature change of equivalent size. Reviewers skim for "does this look reasonable to delete" rather than tracing every removed symbol's actual callers, and CI often can't help because coverage gaps are precisely where dead-code assumptions are wrong — untested code is both the most likely to look unused and the least likely to have a test that fails when it's removed.

Review practices that catch this share one property: they replace assumption with verification. Concretely: require the PR to show *how* unreachability was confirmed — a repo-wide reference search including string-based and dynamic references, not just static call-graph tools; check application logs or APM traces for actual invocation of the code/routes/selectors over a meaningful window (a class or endpoint with zero hits in 30 days of production traffic is a much stronger signal than "I didn't see it referenced"); and treat cross-service or cross-repo usage as in scope — search client apps, mobile builds, and third-party integrations, not just the current repository. For CSS specifically, verify against rendered output across all page variants and A/B or promotional states, not just the default template. Staged rollout matters too: deploy cleanup changes behind a flag or to a canary slice first, and treat "big cleanup PR" as needing the same rollback plan and monitoring window as a feature launch, since the failure mode is a silent removal, not a visible bug.

Finally, org-level habits help: dead code should be marked deprecated and left inert for a release cycle before deletion, with logging added to prove it stayed unused, rather than deleted the moment it's spotted. That turns "I'm pretty sure this isn't used" into "I confirmed this wasn't used," which is the actual bar cleanup work needs to clear.

Cleanup commits fail catastrophically for a specific reason: "dead" and "unused" are judgments about the code as read, not as executed, and the two frequently diverge. Static analysis and grep-based audits see what's referenced in source; they don't see what's referenced by build tooling, feature flags, A/B test cohorts, error-path fallbacks, or conditionally-loaded bundles that only activate under specific runtime conditions. A CSS class with no visible reference in the current codebase may be injected by a third-party script, targeted by a browser extension users rely on, or referenced by a class name constructed via string concatenation that no linter can trace. Code that looks unreachable in the primary flow may be the fallback path for a payment provider timeout that only fires under real-world network conditions rarely seen in staging.

The checkout-flow failure mode specifically tends to involve a few recurring patterns. First, the removed code was reachable via a code path exercised only by a subset of traffic — a particular browser, a particular payment method, a legacy client version still in use, or a redirect-based flow rather than the primary happy path. Second, styling that appeared cosmetic was actually functional — CSS controlling form field visibility, error message display, or JavaScript hooks keyed to class names. Third, the change passed CI because tests exercise the common path, and the deleted logic served an edge case that tests don't cover, either because it predates the test suite or because writing a test for it seemed disproportionate to its apparent importance.

The review practices that catch this share a common thread: they substitute evidence for confidence about what "unused" means. Runtime usage analysis — checking access logs, error tracking, or code-coverage instrumentation in production over a meaningful window, not just staging — is more reliable than static reference-counting, because it captures what actually executes rather than what's textually linked. Grepping for dynamic references (string-built selectors, reflection, template interpolation) before deletion catches cases where static analysis structurally can't see the dependency. Deploying cleanup independently of feature work, in small increments, makes it possible to attribute a regression quickly rather than debugging it inside a larger changeset. Staged rollout with real traffic, rather than an all-at-once deploy, would have surfaced the checkout failure against a fraction of users within minutes instead of hours. And treating any change that touches checkout, auth, or payment surfaces as requiring elevated review — regardless of how trivial the diff looks — closes the gap that "harmless cleanup" language tends to open: the description of a change as low-risk becomes an assumption nobody re-verifies, and the size of a diff gets treated as a proxy for its blast radius when the two are frequently uncorrelated. The fix isn't more caution in general; it's making the review process ask "how do we know this is unused" as an explicit, answerable question rather than an implicit one.

Cleanup commits fail dangerously because "unused" is a claim about the code you can see, not about the system as a whole. A function looks dead if nothing in the repository calls it, but that check misses callers that live outside the searched scope: a build step that references a class by string name, a feature flag that re-enables a code path in certain regions, a background job that only runs on the first of the month, or a mobile client three versions behind still hitting an endpoint the server team assumed was retired. The person doing the cleanup reasons correctly from the evidence in front of them; the evidence is just incomplete, and nothing in a typical diff view flags that.

CSS has its own version of this problem. A selector with zero matches in the current templates can still be targeted by a class name injected at runtime — by a third-party script, an A/B test variant, an email template rendered from the same stylesheet, or JavaScript that constructs class strings dynamically (`"btn-" + variant`) so a text search never turns up the reference. Removing the rule produces no error, no failed build, no red test. It just leaves an element unstyled the next time that code path executes, which might not be until a specific checkout scenario fires hours or days later.

The common thread is that these changes are semantically risky while looking mechanically safe. They pass every check that treats "does the code compile and do the existing tests pass" as sufficient evidence of correctness, because the risk lives in a runtime path the tests don't exercise and the deletion doesn't touch anything the compiler understands as connected.

Review practices that catch this share one property: they substitute broader evidence for local confidence. Concretely:

- Require a dead-code claim to be justified with more than a repo-local grep — check feature-flag configs, string-based references, external callers, and analytics or logs showing whether the code path has fired recently in production.
- Route changes to shared assets (CSS, config, common utility modules) through the teams that own the pages or flows depending on them, rather than treating "no visible caller" as sufficient sign-off from a single reviewer.
- Keep cleanup changes small and separated from feature work, so if something breaks, the change under suspicion is obvious rather than buried in a large diff.
- Roll changes out gradually — behind a flag, to a percentage of traffic, or to a staging environment with realistic data — instead of merging straight to full production traffic, so a broken path shows up as a contained incident rather than an outage.
- Treat "safe because it's just cleanup" as a warning sign itself. Confidence tends to be highest exactly where scrutiny is lowest, since reviewers apply less attention to diffs labeled as low-risk.

None of this requires new tooling so much as recognizing that removing something requires proving a negative — that nothing depends on it — which is a harder claim than adding something new, and deserves review calibrated to that difficulty rather than to how the change reads at a glance.

Cleanup commits fail not because the code they remove is wrong, but because "unused" is a claim about the present, and the present is smaller than the system. A function looks dead if you search the codebase and find no callers, but that search rarely covers everything that actually invokes code in production: feature flags gating a rarely-hit branch, a cron job that runs monthly, a webhook from a third party, a mobile client still on an old version calling an old endpoint, an admin tool nobody documented. The same applies to CSS: a class with no matches in the templates you searched can still be applied by JavaScript that builds class names dynamically, by a string concatenation, by an email template rendered elsewhere, or by a third-party widget injecting markup that expects your styles. Static analysis tools are good at finding references within their own scope and blind to everything outside it.

Checkout flows in particular tend to be exactly the kind of code that looks unused by ordinary reading. They're often reached through conditional paths — a specific payment method, a specific currency, a retry after a failed charge, a fallback for browsers without some capability. A path that fires for five percent of transactions can look, in a quick grep, indistinguishable from a path that fires for zero. The commit author sees no obvious callers and reasonably concludes the code is safe to remove; the five percent shows up only when real traffic arrives.

Three review practices catch this reliably, and none of them are exotic. First, treat deletions with the same scrutiny as additions rather than less — a diff that only removes lines often gets skimmed on the assumption that removal can't introduce new behavior, which is precisely the false assumption that causes these outages. Second, verify "unused" empirically rather than by inspection: instrument the code path with logging or metrics for a full business cycle (not just a day, since some paths only fire weekly or at billing time) and confirm zero invocations before deleting, rather than trusting a text search. Third, stage the removal — deploy behind a flag, or merge but don't release, or delete in a way that fails loud rather than silent, so if something does still depend on the removed code, it surfaces as an immediate, obvious error rather than a slow, confusing symptom discovered by customers.

The deeper practice is cultural: treat "this looks unused" as a hypothesis to test, not a conclusion to act on, especially in revenue-critical paths where the cost of being wrong is measured in hours of downtime rather than a quick revert. Cleanup commits get less scrutiny precisely because they're framed as harmless, which is exactly why they deserve the same pre-deploy validation as any other production change touching checkout.

Splitting a decade-old monolith into microservices via strangler-fig, starting with auth and billing over two quarters, is a sound strategy in principle, but its success depends on several assumptions that are easy to state and hard to verify.

First, the plan assumes the monolith's boundaries around auth and billing are actually separable — that these subsystems don't share database tables, transactions, or implicit invariants (like "billing writes always happen in the same transaction as an auth state change") that would make clean extraction impossible without a deeper untangling effort than scoped for. A decade of accreted code likely has undocumented coupling that won't surface until extraction is underway.

Second, it assumes the team has accurate, current knowledge of the system's behavior. Ten-year-old codebases often outlive the people who understand them; if institutional knowledge has eroded, the "strangler" routing layer will misroute edge cases nobody remembers exist.

Third, it assumes two quarters is enough time not just to write new services but to build the strangler facade, dual-write or dual-read reconciliation, observability for two systems running in parallel, and a rollback path — and that this estimate was built from actual investigation rather than optimism. Migrations chronically underestimate the "glue" work between the old and new systems.

Fourth, choosing auth and billing first assumes these are the right starting points. They're common strangler-fig starting choices because they're well-bounded conceptually, but they're also high-blast-radius: auth failures lock out all users, billing failures have financial and compliance consequences. The plan should assume this risk is acceptable and mitigated, not merely tolerated by default.

Fifth, it assumes data consistency during the transition is solvable — that the team has a concrete answer for how billing state stays correct while both old and new paths can write to it, including reconciliation and idempotency, not just "we'll route traffic gradually."

Sixth, it assumes organizational readiness: that on-call ownership, testing infrastructure, and deployment pipelines for independently-deployable services exist or will be built in parallel, and that engineers have (or will gain) the operational skills microservices demand — this is as much a people and process migration as a technical one.

Seventh, it assumes stakeholders (finance, compliance, customer support) are aligned on acceptable risk and downtime for billing and auth changes specifically, since these are the two subsystems where user-facing incidents are most costly and most visible.

Finally, the plan assumes success can be measured and course-corrected — that there are defined rollback triggers and that "two quarters" is a checkpoint, not a fixed deadline the team will feel pressured to hit even if extraction reveals it's unsafe.

If any of these — separability, institutional knowledge, time realism, blast-radius tolerance, data consistency strategy, org readiness, or stakeholder alignment — doesn't hold, the plan's soundness in principle won't translate into a safe execution in practice.

Assumptions Underlying a Two-Quarter Strangler-Fig Migration (Auth and Billing First)

For this plan to succeed, several load-bearing assumptions need to hold, and most of them are riskier than the timeline implies.

First, the monolith's auth and billing logic must be separable without deep, tangled coupling to other modules. Caching layers between an app and its database exist for reasons the database's internal cache can't address, because they solve a different problem: network and process boundaries, not just disk I/O.

Here's the core distinction. The database's own cache (buffer pool, query cache, whatever the engine calls it) lives inside the database process and speeds up *disk access*. It still requires: a network round-trip from your app server to the database, connection overhead, query parsing and planning, and lock/contention handling on the DB's execution engine. Even a "cache hit" in Postgres or MySQL means the data was already in RAM instead of on disk — but you're still paying for the TCP hop, the SQL parse, and the DB process scheduling your query alongside everyone else's.

An application-level cache (Redis, Memcached, an in-process LRU) sits in front of that entire round-trip. A hit there means zero network calls to the database, zero query execution, zero contention on the DB's connection pool. That's often a 10-100x latency difference from a DB-side cache hit, and it's the difference that matters when a service is doing thousands of requests per second.

There's also a scaling argument. Database connections and query throughput are usually your tightest bottleneck — connection pools are finite, and query execution consumes CPU and I/O on a resource that's expensive to scale horizontally. An external cache lets you absorb read traffic on cheap, horizontally-scalable infrastructure instead of hammering the database every time. If ten app servers each need the same "user profile" object a thousand times a second, you want that served from a shared cache, not from ten thousand round-trips into the database's buffer pool.

A third reason: the caching layer can store things the database cache structurally can't — computed aggregates, joined/denormalized results, rendered API responses, session data, rate-limit counters. The DB cache only accelerates access to raw rows and index pages; it doesn't know about your application's shape of a "product page" that pulls from six tables plus an external pricing service.

None of this means the layer is free — it adds invalidation complexity, another failure mode, and a second source of truth to reason about, which is a completely fair thing to interrogate. If you find specific keys with low hit rates, or reads so infrequent that added complexity isn't earning its keep, that's worth flagging concretely. But "redundant" isn't quite right: they operate at different layers of the stack, solve different bottlenecks (network/process overhead vs. disk I/O), and removing the outer layer would push all that load back onto a resource that's usually the hardest one to scale.

Caching layers and database caches solve different problems, and that's the crux of why removing the application-level cache usually causes regressions rather than simplification.

A database's internal cache (e.g., a buffer pool or query cache) sits close to disk and speeds up repeated *disk reads*. But every request that hits it still has to make a network round trip to the database, acquire connections, parse and plan the query, and consume database CPU and memory. Under load, all of that adds up. An application-level cache — Redis, Memcached, an in-process cache — avoids the round trip entirely for cache hits. The difference isn't marginal: a local or network cache lookup is typically sub-millisecond, while even a "fast" indexed database query is often 5-50x slower once you account for connection overhead and query execution. At scale, that gap is the difference between a database that keeps up and one that falls over.

There's also a capacity argument. Databases have a finite connection pool and finite CPU. Every query you can serve from a cache is a query the database doesn't have to plan, execute, or lock resources for. If you remove the caching layer, you're not just adding latency — you're shifting load back onto a component that's usually your hardest system to scale horizontally. Application servers and cache nodes scale out cheaply; databases, especially relational ones, do not.

Caches also let you store *derived* or *aggregated* data — the result of an expensive join, a computed recommendation, a rendered API response — that the database's cache can't help with at all, because the database cache only speads up re-reading the same rows, not re-doing the same computation.

That said, the instinct to question it is a good one, because caching layers are genuinely expensive in complexity: cache invalidation, staleness bugs, and "which layer is lying to us" debugging sessions are real costs. So the right question isn't "is this redundant" but "is this cache pulling its weight relative to that complexity." Worth checking:

- What's the actual cache hit rate? If it's low (say, under 60-70%), it may be misconfigured or caching the wrong things, and it's fair to ask whether it's earning its keep.
- What's the latency and load difference measured with it on vs. off, under realistic traffic?
- Is it caching expensive computed results, or just raw rows the DB cache already handles well? If the latter, there may be real overlap worth trimming.

Caching layers get proposed for removal a lot, usually right after someone reads that Postgres or MySQL already caches pages in memory. The intuition is reasonable but misses what the two caches are actually for.

The database's internal cache — its buffer pool — exists to avoid disk I/O for pages it has already read. It's scoped to a single database instance, keyed on physical storage layout, and evicted according to the database's own memory pressure. It has no idea what a "query result" is, let alone what your application logic is going to do with one. It just remembers raw pages.

Our caching layer sits at a completely different altitude. It stores computed, application-level artifacts — a serialized API response, an aggregation across three tables, a value pulled from an external service — keyed by something meaningful to the app (a user ID, a cache-busting version string, a request signature). Even when the buffer pool has every relevant page in memory, the database still has to parse the query, plan it, execute the joins, and serialize rows back across the wire. That's real CPU and network time our cache skips entirely by returning a value with no query at all.

There's also a blast-radius argument. When the database is slow — a lock contention spike, a bad plan after a stats update, a replica falling behind — the buffer pool doesn't protect you, because it's part of the thing that's struggling. Our cache, being a separate process, keeps serving traffic through that window. Removing it means every performance problem downstream becomes a performance problem for every caller upstream, immediately.

Scale matters too. The buffer pool is sized to one machine's RAM and one workload. Our cache can be sharded, replicated, and scaled independently of the database, so it absorbs traffic spikes without forcing us to vertically scale the database itself — which is expensive and has a ceiling.

None of this means the layer is beyond question. It's fair to ask whether the TTLs are right, whether we're caching things nobody rereads, whether invalidation bugs are costing us more correctness than the hit rate is worth, or whether a given endpoint should just have been backed by an index instead of a cache entry. Those are real, useful reviews. But the argument "the database already caches" isn't one of them — it compares a page cache to an application cache as if they did the same job. They don't overlap much at all: one saves disk reads, the other saves entire round trips of computation and query execution. If you removed it, you would not get the same system with one redundant part gone; you would get a database that now has to do everything the cache used to do, for every single request, with no separate layer left to fall over to when it can't keep up.

That last point is the real reason removal is dangerous, not just slow. A module like `config/legacy_flags.py` is dangerous to delete precisely because the dependencies that matter are the ones static analysis cannot see. Start by enumerating the invisible coupling paths.

The first is import-time side effects. A flags module often does more than define constants: it may register defaults into a global registry, monkey-patch a library, set environment variables, seed a random number generator, or populate a singleton on first import. If any module imports it purely for those effects, grep for symbol names will show zero references while removal still changes runtime behavior. Check the module body for anything executed at import rather than merely defined.

The second is dynamic access. Flags are frequently read through `getattr(config, name)`, dictionary lookups keyed by strings, `importlib.import_module`, Django-style settings indirection, or serialized names coming from a database, YAML file, feature-flag service, or admin UI. A grep for `legacy_flags` misses every one of these. Search instead for the individual flag names as bare strings across the whole repository, plus infrastructure repos, Helm charts, Terraform, CI configs, and any sibling services.

Third is cross-repo and out-of-process consumers. If the package is published internally, other teams may import it. Analytics jobs, notebooks, cron scripts, one-off migration tooling, and disaster-recovery runbooks live outside the main codebase and outside CI, so their breakage surfaces late and at the worst time.

Fourth is behavioral inversion. The riskiest flag is one whose default is "off" but which some environment sets to "on," or a kill-switch that has been dormant for years and exists exactly for an emergency nobody has needed yet. Deleting it removes an escape hatch rather than dead code.

For assessment, prefer evidence over reasoning. Ranked roughly by strength: add runtime instrumentation — log or emit a metric on module import and on each flag read — then let it run through at least one full business cycle, including month-end and quarter-end batch jobs, before concluding it is unused. Weaker but cheap signals include coverage data from production-like traffic, `git log` archaeology to learn why each flag was introduced, and repo-wide string searches.

The safe removal sequence is deprecate, observe, then delete: keep the module but make every access loud, ship that, wait, and only remove once the telemetry is silent across a full cycle. Delete in a single revertable commit, behind a release you can roll back quickly, and not immediately before a freeze or a holiday. If instrumentation is impossible, the honest answer is that the risk is unquantified — and unquantified risk on a 400-line module is usually not worth taking this quarter.

Silent dependencies on a module like `config/legacy_flags.py` fall into categories that static reasoning about imports will not surface. The most common is dynamic access: `importlib.import_module`, `__import__`, `getattr` on a settings object, or a string-keyed registry that resolves flag names at runtime. A grep for `legacy_flags` catches literal imports but misses `import_module(f"config.{name}")`. Equally common is import-for-side-effect — the module may register signal handlers, populate a global registry, monkeypatch a third-party default, set environment variables, or seed a singleton at import time. If any other module imports it purely for those effects, the import statement looks vestigial and the deletion looks safe right up until a default silently changes in production.

Second, configuration modules tend to be read by things that are not Python. Deployment templates, Ansible or Terraform files, Docker entrypoints, CI jobs, and ops runbooks may reference flag names as strings. Serialized state is worse: if flag values were ever pickled, cached, or written into database rows, feature-flag tables, or user preference blobs, removal changes deserialization behavior rather than raising an error. Frameworks add their own path — Django settings modules, pytest conftest chains, plugin entry points declared in `setup.py`/`pyproject.toml`, and Celery task registries all load modules by name from configuration rather than by import.

Third, the module may be doing nothing visible but supplying fallbacks. Four hundred lines of defaults matter only when the primary configuration source is absent — which is precisely the rare path: disaster recovery, a fresh environment, a degraded upstream, a batch job that runs quarterly. Absence of traffic through the code is weak evidence when the code exists to handle absence.

Risk assessment therefore should combine several independent signals rather than trusting any one. Search the whole organization, not the repo: every service, infra repo, notebook, and scheduled job, for the module path and for individual flag names as bare strings. Read the module's git history and blame to recover intent — the commit that added each flag usually names the incident it was for. Instrument before deleting: add import-time and attribute-access logging (a module `__getattr__` works well), ship it, and let it run through at least one full business cycle including month-end and any quarterly jobs. Check whether the module has meaningful test coverage, since untested code is both likelier to be dead and likelier to break unnoticed.

Then prefer a reversible sequence: deprecate with warnings, then raise on access, then delete — each step behind a release that can be rolled back cheaply. The cost of a staged removal is a few weeks; the cost of a silent default change discovered during an incident is much higher.

Cleanup commits are dangerous precisely because of how they are framed. "Removes dead code and unused CSS" carries an implicit claim — that the removed things were provably unreachable — and reviewers tend to accept that claim rather than test it. The diff is large, uniformly deletions, and individually boring, so attention drops exactly where it is most needed. Risk perception is inverted: the commit that adds a feature gets scrutiny, the one that only subtracts gets a thumbs-up.

The underlying failure is that "unused" is a claim about the whole system, and most tools that answer it only see part of the system. Static analysis of a codebase cannot see reflection, dynamic dispatch, string-built identifiers, feature flags, server-rendered markup, template interpolation, or configuration that names a symbol at runtime. CSS is worse still: coverage tooling reports what was unused during the pages and states it happened to observe. A checkout flow is mostly states that a crawler never reaches — error banners, declined-payment messaging, address validation, the third-party payment iframe, a regional variant that only renders for some customers. A rule that appears unused on the happy path may be the only thing giving a critical button its dimensions when an error state renders.

Cleanup also removes things that were load-bearing by accident. Code that looks dead may be keeping a module imported, a side effect firing, a polyfill registered, or a bundle chunk present. Removing an apparently redundant wrapper element can change specificity, stacking context, or layout in ways nothing tests. And cleanup diffs often mix genuinely dead code with code that is merely unfamiliar, because the person doing the cleaning is typically the person with the least history in that area.

The timeline matters too. Deletion-caused failures are frequently invisible at deploy and only appear in a state that a fraction of users reach, which is why detection takes hours rather than minutes, and why the cleanup commit is the last thing anyone suspects.

Practices that actually catch this: require evidence, not assertion — the author states how each deletion was proven unreachable, and reviewers treat unsupported claims as blocking. Separate cleanup from behavioral change, and keep each cleanup commit small and revertible so bisecting is cheap. Grep for symbol names as strings, not just as identifiers. Route deletions to owners of the affected flow rather than any available reviewer. For revenue paths, insist that end-to-end tests exercise failure and edge states, not just successful purchase. Ship cleanup behind the same staged rollout and monitoring as anything else, and prefer deprecating with telemetry for a release before deleting outright.

Cleanup commits carry a specific and underappreciated risk: they are defined by what they remove, and removal is the one class of change whose failure modes are invisible in the diff itself. When you add a function, the reviewer can read it and reason about whether it is correct. When you delete one, correctness depends entirely on facts that are not on the screen — who else called it, what referenced that CSS class, what the runtime does when the selector no longer matches. The usual mechanism is a gap between static reachability and actual reachability. Code looks dead because no static reference exists, but it is reached through something the analyzer cannot follow: a string-based dispatch table, reflection, a dynamic import, a feature flag evaluated at runtime, a webhook or cron entry that names a handler in configuration rather than in code, a template rendered by a different service. Checkout flows are unusually rich in exactly these patterns — payment provider callbacks, third-party scripts keyed to DOM hooks, A/B test branches, error and retry paths that only execute on the unhappy path.

Unused CSS is the same problem in a different dialect. A class can be absent from every template you can grep and still be applied at runtime by JavaScript, by a CMS field, by an email template, or by a vendor widget. And CSS failures are quietly severe: a removed rule does not throw. The page renders, the button is simply invisible, or overlapped, or the overlay that traps clicks never gets its z-index. No error surfaces, no exception is logged, so alerting sees a healthy service while conversion silently goes to zero. The three-hour duration is the real tell here — not that something broke, but that nothing screamed.

Cleanup also arrives socially disarmed. It is labeled harmless, it touches many files shallowly, and reviewers pattern-match on the label rather than the content. A thousand-line deletion gets less scrutiny than a fifty-line feature, precisely inverted from the risk.

Practices that catch this: treat deletions as behavioral changes and hold them to the same testing bar as features. Keep cleanup commits separate from functional ones and small enough to bisect. Require the author to state, per removal, the evidence it is dead — not "grep found nothing" but runtime evidence: telemetry showing zero hits over a meaningful window, coverage data, logs from a deprecation shim left in place for a release cycle. Prefer a two-step retirement — instrument, wait, then delete. Run visual regression and end-to-end tests through the actual revenue path, since those are the only checks that detect a missing style rule. Ship behind a flag or canary so blast radius is bounded. And add synthetic monitoring of the funnel itself, so a silent visual break registers as an incident rather than a slow bleed someone notices hours later.

For styling, rely on visual regression testing and real end-to-end tests through checkout rather than unit tests, since layout breakage is silent. The practices that catch this are mostly about replacing inference with evidence. Route deletions touching revenue paths to owners who know the history. Treat CSS as dynamically referenced by default and verify visually across real checkout states, including error and edge-case renders. Finally, ship cleanups behind the same progressive rollout and monitoring as features, and define what a checkout regression looks like in your dashboards before you need to spot one.

Cleanup commits fail in production for a reason that has little to do with the code being removed and everything to do with how "unused" gets established. The tooling that flags dead code reasons over static references: it can see that no source file names a function, no template quotes a class. A function reached only through reflection, a dependency-injection registry, or an event name matched by convention. A style rule that a third-party payment iframe or an A/B testing script targets from outside the repository entirely. Each of these looks orphaned from the compiler's vantage point and is anything but from the browser's.

Removal tools measure frequency, and rarity reads as death. The CSS variant of this is nastier still, because deleting a rule usually produces no error at all: the button simply renders with zero height, or the overlay stops receiving pointer events, and everything continues to report success while no one can pay.

The second contributor is how these changes get reviewed. A diff that is entirely deletions invites a different reading posture than one that adds behavior. Reviewers skim, the description says "no functional change," and the size of the diff becomes evidence of harmlessness rather than a reason for scrutiny. Cleanup also tends to be batched, so a hundred small removals share one approval, and nothing in the process forces a per-item justification.

What catches this is mostly procedural. Split cleanup from feature work so it can be reverted cleanly and bisected quickly. Route it through the same staged rollout and canary period as any behavioral change, since it is one. Prefer a deprecation window over immediate removal: annotate, log when the supposedly dead path executes, wait a full billing or seasonal cycle, then delete what stayed silent. Finally, gate revenue-critical flows behind end-to-end tests that actually complete a transaction, so a missing style rule fails a check rather than a customer.
